description: Designing systems where correctness depends on timing as well as results: hard and soft deadlines, real-time operating systems, fixed- and dynamic-priority scheduling, synchronisation and priority inversion, worst-case timing analysis, real-time communication, and the design of safety-critical software. Taught with browser-based simulations of a real-time scheduler and task sets, so students run schedules, inject timing faults and measure response times without physical hardware.
modelledOn: Burns and Wellings, Real-Time Systems and Programming Languages
outcomes: Distinguish hard, firm and soft real-time requirements and state tasks as periodic, sporadic or aperiodic with deadlines.
Select and configure a real-time operating system and explain how it bounds latency.
Apply rate-monotonic and earliest-deadline-first scheduling and test a task set for schedulability.
Diagnose priority inversion and apply priority inheritance and ceiling protocols to shared resources.
Compute worst-case execution and response times and reason about jitter and overload.
Design communication and safety-critical architectures that meet timing and dependability requirements.

units.title: Real-time requirements and deadlines
topics: What makes a system real-time: timing as a correctness condition, not just performance
Hard, firm and soft deadlines; value-versus-time functions and the cost of a miss
Task models: periodic, sporadic and aperiodic tasks; period, deadline, release and execution time
Metrics: response time, latency, jitter, throughput and utilisation
Examples across domains: engine control, a mobile-money transaction switch under load, medical monitors

units.title: Real-time operating systems
topics: General-purpose versus real-time operating systems; sources of unbounded latency in a general-purpose kernel
The real-time kernel: task control blocks, states, the ready queue and the dispatcher
Preemptive priority scheduling, context-switch cost and tick-based versus tickless timing
Interrupt handling, deferred work and interrupt latency
Clocks, timers and time representation; measuring kernel overhead in the simulator

units.title: Fixed-priority scheduling: rate monotonic
topics: Fixed-priority preemptive scheduling and priority assignment
Rate-monotonic priority assignment and its optimality among fixed-priority schemes
The utilisation bound test and its sufficiency but not necessity
Deadline-monotonic assignment when deadlines differ from periods
Running task sets in the simulator and observing missed deadlines at high utilisation

units.title: Dynamic-priority scheduling: earliest deadline first
topics: Earliest-deadline-first scheduling and its optimality for preemptive single-processor systems
The EDF utilisation test and comparison with rate monotonic
Least-laxity-first and other dynamic schemes
Behaviour under transient overload: domino effect in EDF versus graceful degradation
Admission control and handling aperiodic work with servers

units.title: Synchronisation and priority inversion
topics: Shared resources, critical sections and mutual exclusion in a real-time context
Unbounded priority inversion: how a low-priority task blocks a high-priority one
The priority-inheritance protocol and its limits
The priority-ceiling and immediate-ceiling protocols; bounding blocking time and preventing deadlock
Accounting for blocking in a schedulability test
Reproducing a priority-inversion failure in the simulator and fixing it

units.title: Worst-case timing analysis
topics: Worst-case execution time: why average time is not enough for hard deadlines
Measurement-based and static analysis of execution time; the effect of caches and pipelines
Response-time analysis: the recurrence for a task's worst-case response under interference
Accounting for release jitter, blocking and context-switch overhead
Sensitivity analysis and headroom; what to do when a set is not schedulable

units.title: Real-time communication
topics: Timing on a shared medium; bounding message latency and jitter
Priority-based and time-triggered buses; the controller area network arbitration scheme
Time-triggered and time-sensitive networking; clock synchronisation across nodes
End-to-end deadlines across a distributed system and holistic analysis
Degradation under a congested or lossy link, as on intermittent West Africa backhaul

units.title: Safety-critical design
topics: Dependability: reliability, availability, safety and the difference between faults, errors and failures
Hazard analysis and safety integrity levels; fail-safe and fail-operational design
Redundancy, watchdogs, and detecting a missed deadline or a hung task
Handling power cuts and brown-outs with safe shutdown and an uninterruptible supply
Certification evidence and the role of standards in safety-critical software

units.title: Designing and evaluating a real-time system
topics: Putting it together: task decomposition, priority assignment, resource protocols and timing budget
Validating a design by schedulability analysis and by simulation
Diagnosing overload, jitter and inversion from traces
Capstone: specify, schedule and verify a small safety-critical controller under a fixed timing budget

schedule.title: What makes a system real-time
schedule.exercise: Classify ten systems (airbag, ATM, video call, drone, mobile-money switch) as hard, firm or soft real-time, and draw the value-versus-time curve for three of them.

tasks.title: Enter three periodic tasks with period, deadline and execution time into the scheduler visualiser and read the first 20 time units of the timeline
Classify the deadline type of eight embedded systems and decide the cost of a miss for each, scored against the rubric
Model a task set that includes one sporadic and one aperiodic task and show what happens to a periodic deadline when the sporadic task arrives in a burst

schedule.title: Timing metrics and examples
schedule.exercise: For a pressure sensor sampled every 10 ms, compute response time, latency and jitter from a trace of 20 samples and state whether a 50 ms deadline is met.

tasks.title: Read a given task timeline and calculate each task's response time and CPU utilisation, recording both in a table
Toggle an Arduino pin from a timer interrupt every 10 ms and measure the jitter of 50 pulses on the simulated logic analyser
Simulate a mobile-money switch with random arrivals at increasing load and plot the 99th percentile response time against utilisation

schedule.title: Real-time kernels and interrupts
schedule.exercise: Compare a general-purpose and a real-time kernel on sources of latency, and trace by hand the dispatcher actions when a higher-priority task becomes ready during a lower one's execution.

tasks.title: Step through the kernel visualiser for three tasks and record each task's state (ready, running, blocked) at every tick for 15 ticks
Run preemptive priority scheduling with and without context-switch cost and compare the number of missed deadlines in each run
Measure interrupt latency on a simulated microcontroller with a competing interrupt, and design a handler that defers the long work to a task

schedule.title: Fixed-priority scheduling
schedule.exercise: Assign rate-monotonic priorities to four periodic tasks, compute utilisation, compare with the Liu-Layland bound, and explain why failing the bound does not prove unschedulability.

tasks.title: Assign rate-monotonic priorities to three tasks with periods 5, 10 and 20 and verify in the visualiser that every deadline is met
Compute total utilisation and the Liu-Layland bound for five task sets and state for each whether the test passes, fails or is inconclusive
Find a task set that fails the utilisation bound yet meets every deadline in simulation, and explain why using the timeline

schedule.title: Deadline-monotonic and overload behaviour
schedule.exercise: For a task set where deadlines are shorter than periods, assign deadline-monotonic priorities, compare with rate-monotonic, and show which one meets all deadlines.

tasks.title: Assign deadline-monotonic priorities to four tasks with deadlines shorter than periods and run the schedule to confirm deadlines are met
Raise task execution times until utilisation passes 90 percent, and record the first deadline miss and which task suffers it
Build a task set where rate-monotonic misses a deadline but deadline-monotonic meets every one, and present both timelines side by side

schedule.title: Dynamic priority scheduling
schedule.exercise: Schedule a task set with utilisation 0.95 under EDF and rate-monotonic by hand over one hyperperiod, and explain the transient overload behaviour of each.

tasks.title: Run EDF on three tasks with utilisation 0.9 in the visualiser and confirm all deadlines are met over one hyperperiod
Run a task set with utilisation 0.95 under EDF and rate-monotonic, and compare which meets every deadline and the number of preemptions
Apply a transient overload to EDF and rate-monotonic schedules and show how the domino effect appears in one and not the other

schedule.title: Shared resources and priority inversion
schedule.exercise: Draw the timeline of three tasks sharing a mutex that produces unbounded priority inversion, and show how priority inheritance bounds the blocking.

tasks.title: Run two tasks sharing a mutex in the visualiser and mark the critical section and the time the higher-priority task waits
Create three tasks that cause unbounded priority inversion on a shared mutex and record the high-priority task's blocking time
Enable priority inheritance on the inversion case and compare the blocking time, then construct a case where inheritance still allows chained blocking

schedule.title: Ceiling protocols and blocking analysis
schedule.exercise: Compute the maximum blocking time of each task under the priority-ceiling protocol from a table of critical section lengths, and re-run the response-time test including blocking.

tasks.title: Assign ceilings to three shared resources from the tasks that use them and run the ceiling protocol to confirm no deadlock occurs
Compute the worst-case blocking for each of four tasks under the immediate-ceiling protocol and add it to the schedulability test
Reproduce a Mars-Pathfinder-style priority-inversion failure in the simulator, diagnose it from the trace, and fix it with the right protocol

schedule.title: Execution time and response-time analysis
schedule.exercise: Explain why average execution time is not safe for a hard deadline, and compute the worst-case response time of the lowest-priority task in a four-task set using the recurrence.

tasks.title: Measure execution time of a given routine over 100 runs with varied inputs on the simulated board and report the mean and the maximum observed
Apply response-time analysis iteration to a four-task set, record each iteration of the recurrence, and decide whether each task meets its deadline
Show how a cache miss pattern changes execution time in the cache visualiser, and choose a safe WCET bound with a stated margin

schedule.title: Overheads, jitter and sensitivity
schedule.exercise: Add release jitter, blocking and context-switch overhead to a response-time analysis and find how much each task's execution time can grow before a deadline is missed.

tasks.title: Add a 0.2 ms context-switch cost to each task in a response-time table and recompute the response times to see which change
Scale all execution times by a factor until the first deadline miss and report the breakdown factor for a given four-task set
Fix an unschedulable five-task set by changing periods, execution budgets or priorities within stated limits, and show the fixed timeline

schedule.title: Real-time communication and distribution
schedule.exercise: Compute the worst-case latency of the lowest-priority message on a CAN bus with three message streams, and the end-to-end delay of a sensor to actuator path across two nodes.

tasks.title: Send three CAN messages of different identifiers at once on the simulated bus and record which wins arbitration in what order
Compute the worst-case response time of each of four periodic CAN messages including blocking by a lower-priority frame
Simulate a sensor-to-actuator path over a lossy link with 5 and 20 percent loss and report how often the end-to-end deadline is missed

schedule.title: Dependability and safety
schedule.exercise: Perform a simple hazard analysis of an infusion pump controller, assign a safety integrity level to each hazard, and describe the watchdog and redundancy measures you would add.

tasks.title: Add a watchdog timer to a simulated microcontroller loop, then hang the loop deliberately and observe the reset
Carry out a hazard analysis on a vehicle brake controller case, rank the hazards and choose mitigations, and score against the rubric
Design a brown-out detector that saves state and shuts a simulated controller down safely, and test it with three supply-drop profiles

schedule.title: Capstone: design and verify a controller
schedule.exercise: Document a design for a small safety-critical controller (for example a grain-dryer temperature controller): task table, priorities, resource protocol, timing budget and verification evidence.

tasks.title: Decompose a described controller into five periodic tasks, assign rate-monotonic priorities, and verify the resulting schedule in the visualiser
Diagnose from a recorded trace whether the missed deadline comes from overload, jitter or priority inversion, and justify your finding
Specify, schedule and verify a grain-dryer controller within a 2 ms timing budget using response-time analysis and simulation, and confirm both agree
